newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to push Mideast peace despite Israel crisis.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to push Mideast peace despite Israel crisis.

text.p: The United States vowed on Thursday to press ahead with Middle East peace efforts despite an Israeli political crisis that analysts said could further delay attempts to get stalled negotiations back on track.

The White House said it was up to the Israelis to resolve the corruption scandal which broke on Wednesday around Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as U.S. envoy Dennis Ross held talks in the region with Israeli and Palestinian leaders.
"We consider this a domestic legal matter that the Israeli government and the people of Israel have to resolve," White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said.
Netanyahu refused to quit Thursday after police announced they had recommended he be tried for fraud and breach of trust over the appointment of an Israeli attorney-general.
Asked if the uproar would delay peace efforts, McCurry said: "I'm not going to speculate on that. We will remain committed to doing our best to press forward in the Middle East peace process."

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the United States was "determined to make as much progress as we can." Ross returns home at the weekend to report to President Bill Clinton and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who will decide the next steps.

Ross is trying to revive Israeli-Palestinian peace talks stalled over an Israeli decision last month to start a Jewish housing project in traditionally Arab East Jerusalem. The move has sparked almost daily Palestinian demonstrations.

"We are determined to move forward," Burns told a news briefing. "We do think it's important to continue the talks with the Israelis and Palestinians. I don't believe they are going to stop because there is a political crisis."
But he added: "It's very good tough going, obviously, because of the profound disagreement between the Israelis and Palestinians."
The Palestinians have insisted that Israel stop work on the housing project, on a hill known to Jews as Har Homa and to Arabs as Jabal Abu Ghneim, before they will resume talks.
Despite the administration's resolve to soldier on, U.S. analysts and commentators said they believed the Israeli crisis would delay attempts to get the peace process moving again.
"It will push (U.S. mediators) into more of a wait-and-see approach," one analyst close to the administration said.
Another expert, Saadia Touval of the Paul Nitze School of Advanced International Studies in Washington, said he saw advantages and disadvantages in the affair.
"Right now, if Netanyahu were to be indicted, then it will be a long process for him to resign, and elections to be held, and in this respect it would be a setback," Touval said.

"In the long run, if Labour were to gain power, then the peace process would go faster," he added. The Labour Party has been much more open to concessions to the Palestinians than Netanyahu's Likud Party, which took power last year.
The Clinton administration came close to openly backing Labour in last May's elections, and analysts said there would be some U.S. officials who would be glad to see Netanyahu unseated.

But the New York Times said the Israeli crisis "can only complicate attempts to rescue the troubled peace with the Palestinians, which is nearer collapse now than at any time since the Oslo agreements were signed nearly four years ago."
"The necessary decisions for peace can only be made by an Israeli government whose own legitimacy remains above doubt," the newspaper said in an editorial.
